To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
anionic guanine tautomeric structures with a pi orbital occupied by excess electrons have higher stability than the corresponding neutral species.
anionic tautomeric structures of guanine have been identified and analyzed in two ways: by hologram analysis of quantum chemical data and by substructure analysis and 2D clustering of the tautomers.

the high stability and the homogenous excess electron distribution of adiabatic anions of guanines are caused by the bonding character of pi orbitals occupied by the excess electrons, which compensates for the usual antibonding character.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of the sources of stability of anionic guanine and the analysis of the chemical space of its tautomers.
the discovery of new chemical species that might have biological significance and with the development of new computational methods that could be applied to other chemical systems.
the discovery of anionic tautomer(s) that might be involved, in the processes of electron transfer through DNA and in DNA damage by low energy electrons.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the anionic tautomeric species of guanine are not just the "abnormal" forms of the most stable guanine neutrals.
the adiabatic electron attachment to guanine results in a tautomeric shift that involves the loss of hydrogen atoms at C4, C6, and C5 and their attachment to C8 and C2.
adiabatically formed anionic tautomeric species of guanine are stabilized by the bonding character of singly occupied molecular orbitals and they are contained in a subspace of guanine tautomerism.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the adiabatic binding energy of an excess electron to guanine is determined by the bonding character of pi orbitals and that the most stable anions of guanines form an "islet" of stability in the tautomers space.
the excess electron in anions of guanines can be accommodated by the pi orbital of guanines.
the adiabatic anions of guanines are stable due to their bonding character of the singly occupied molecular orbital (SOMO) and the homogenously distributed excess electron.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the excess electron in anionic tautomeric forms of guanine is more delocalized over both rings, which compensates for the loss of bonding character of the occupied pi orbital.
anionic guanine tautomeric space is different from the neutrals' space and that this difference is caused by the presence of an excess electron.
the tautomeric subspace of the most stable guanine anion is different from that of the most stable species.
